MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF 
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) moves for leave and submits this 
answer1 in support of the Commission’s preliminary finding that the PJM Tariff is unjust and 
unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and preferential2 because, as recent filings plainly show, 
no one knows the rules for the co-location of large loads and generation.  That lack of clarity is 
allowing certain transmission owners to erect discriminatory roadblocks to safe and reliable 
interconnection configurations that would reduce the need for costly transmission upgrades and 
preserve each state’s jurisdiction to decide how to regulate sales to end-use customers.  The need 
for clarity in the tariff cannot wait any longer.  President Trump has emphasized that the United 
States’ competitiveness with other nations depends on the development of Artificial Intelligence 
(“AI”) infrastructure and that co-location enables such development “on a very rapid basis.”3  
 
1 Constellation submits this answer and motion for leave pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules 
of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213, and respectfully submits there is good cause for the 
Commission to accept the motion for leave.  See Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) 
(accepting answers that “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making”); 
Saltville Gas Storage Co., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in 
understanding the issues raised[] and will ensure a complete record”). 
2 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 74 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”). 
3 The White House, Remarks by President Trump at the World Economic Forum, January 23, 2025, 11-12, 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/remarks/2025/01/remarks-by-president-trump-at-the-world-economic-forum/.

2 
Accordingly, the Commission should affirm its preliminary finding and fix a replacement rate by 
adopting rules for a variety of co-location configurations as already fully supported in the record. 
 
THE RECORD CONCLUSIVELY DEMONSTRATES THAT THE PJM TARIFF 
IS UNJUST AND UNREASONABLE 
This is “a show cause proceeding pursuant to section 206” of the Federal Power Act 
(“FPA”)4 which includes “a two-step procedure that requires … an explicit finding that the existing 
rate is unlawful before setting a new rate.”5  Thus, as a threshold matter, the Commission must 
first “determine whether an existing [rule] is ‘unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or 
preferential….’”6  The Commission initiated this proceeding with a preliminary finding under 
section 206 of the FPA that 
the existing PJM Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable or unduly 
discriminatory or preferential because it does not contain provisions addressing 
with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that 
apply to co-location arrangements.  The absence of such provisions may leave 
entities unable to determine what steps they can or must take to effectuate co-
location arrangements of various configurations and how to do so in a manner that 
is just and reasonable.7  
 
The approximately fifty filings submitted in response to the Show Cause Order conclusively 
demonstrate the correctness of the Commission’s preliminary finding. 
 
4 Show Cause Order at P 2; see 16 U.S.C. § 824e. 
5 Emera Me. v. FERC, 854 F.3d 9, 24 (D.C. Cir. 2017); see also MISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 45 F.4th 248, 
253 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (“At step one, FERC decides if the old rate is unjust and unreasonable. … If so, then FERC 
proceeds to step two and sets a new rate.”) (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a)). 
6 Emera Me., 854 F.3d at 21 (quoting 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a)).  In determining whether the existing rate is unreasonable, 
the evidence must be “assessed in light of the FPA’s goals of promoting reliable service at reasonable rates and

Of the remaining filing parties who addressed the issue whether the PJM Tariff is just and 
reasonable, only two parties and two individuals are outliers that did not advocate for any Tariff

there is none.29   
In sum, the record in this proceeding unequivocally supports the Commission’s preliminary 
finding that the PJM Tariff lacks clear co-location rules and is unjust and unreasonable.  Again,

One of the most fundamental elements of just and reasonable rates is that customers must 
know the rate in advance.32  “Predictability” is a “central purpose of the filed rate doctrine.”33  
Review of the filings in this case highlights nearly universal acknowledgement that the PJM Tariff 
lacks “predictable” co-location rules.  Accordingly, and consistent with Commission precedent, 
the Commission must find that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because, first and 
foremost, no one knows the rules.34

[clear co-location] provisions may leave entities unable to determine what steps they can or must

In response to the Show Cause Order, Constellation included extensive record evidence 
supported by sworn expert testimony of the significant injury the lack of clear co-location rules 
and delays in service to data centers are causing to economic and national security, and the host of 
other injuries inflicted by the current de facto NITS-only approach (including billions of dollars of 
unnecessary transmission upgrades, intrusion on state jurisdictional authority and flexibility, and 
violation of cost-causation and other rate design fundamentals).37  No expert rebuttal to any of this 
evidence was filed by the Indicated Transmission Owners or any other opponent in response to the 
Show Cause Order, and argument in pleadings without an evidentiary basis is insufficient to rebut 
record evidence.38  Many parties not only failed to submit any expert analysis to demonstrate why 
the current PJM Tariff is just and reasonable but also failed to respond to the Commission’s 
briefing questions contained in the Show Cause Order.   
Based on the record, the Commission should affirm its preliminary finding under section 
206 of the FPA that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it lacks “provisions 
addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that 
apply to co-location arrangements.”39

10 
 
THE RECORD SUPPORTS THE COMMISSION’S ADOPTION OF A 
REPLACEMENT RATE OF CO-LOCATION CONFIGURATION OPTIONS 
With the step one showing made under section 206 of the FPA, the Commission must move 
to step two and fix a replacement rate.  Under the plain terms of the FPA, the Commission has no 
discretion to do otherwise.  The record in this proceeding already does the heavy lifting and 
provides substantial evidence and support for adopting new “generator-contingent” options (PJM 
Options 4 and 5) and a provisional “interruptible” option (PJM Option 7), as well as clarifying the 
Tariff to allow a “firm” co-location configuration based on net generation and load at a point of 
interconnection (PJM Option 2, which essentially would clarify that the same rules for PJM Option 
3 should be available at the co-located load and generator’s election).  With appropriate rate 
treatment as demonstrated in the record, these three categories of potential co-location 
configurations collectively provide a just and reasonable rate that maximizes efficient use of 
existing energy infrastructure and minimizes expansive transmission upgrades and other costs.  
Each type of configuration also appropriately allocates costs commensurate with the level of 
transmission service being used by the load.  Constellation introduced extensive record support for
